Iambic pentameter is a metrical pattern in English poetry consisting of five iambic feet per line. Each iamb is an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable, creating a ten-syllable rhythm. It became the standard meter of English dramatic verse and remained dominant in lyric poetry from the Renaissance through the nineteenth century. Because of its natural alignment with English speech patterns, it became the closest thing English has to a default poetic line.

Each iamb contains two syllables: unstressed-STRESSED, and pentameter means five feet per line, yielding ten syllables total. The pattern is most recognizable in Shakespeare's plays and sonnets, such as in the line Shall I compare thee to a summer's day. The regular rhythm mirrors natural English speech more closely than most meters, making iambic pentameter feel both formal and conversational. Variations and substitutions—trochaic feet, spondees—within the pattern allow poets to avoid monotony and emphasize particular words.

Heroic couplets, pairs of rhymed iambic pentameter lines, were the dominant form for narrative poetry, especially in seventeenth and eighteenth-century satire and epic. Pope's Essay on Criticism exemplifies the form's satiric power. Sonnets are defined partly by their use of iambic pentameter, which creates the tonal elevation and formal beauty the form demands. Milton's Paradise Lost uses iambic pentameter in unrhymed form, known as blank verse, establishing it as the meter for philosophical and narrative weight.

The pentameter line's ten syllables map imperfectly onto English stress patterns, creating productive tension between metrical regularity and natural speech rhythm. This flexibility is part of the form's power. In performance, iambic pentameter creates a hypnotic regularity that makes departures from the norm resonate. A spondee or trochee in place of an expected iamb draws the ear's attention to a key word. Poetry as a broader metrical tradition is shaped by iambic pentameter. Versification, the technical study of metrical patterns, counts iambic pentameter as the most historically dominant form. The sonnet's identity is inseparable from iambic pentameter's ten-syllable rhythm. The heroic couplet as a rhymed form became the vehicle for satire and narrative. William Shakespeare is the poet and dramatist most associated with the form's elevation and flexibility. The English Renaissance was the period when iambic pentameter became the standard of English verse. Blank verse, iambic pentameter without rhyme, was pioneered in English by Surrey and perfected by Milton.
